title: Decisions and loops
objective: By the end of this lesson your scripts can check a condition before acting, repeat work across a list, and stop early when something is wrong.

blocks.text: A script that runs the same commands regardless of what it finds is a recording. A script that checks first is a tool. Two structures cover almost everything: ask a question, and repeat over a list.

blocks.caption: The shape
lines: echo "That is a directory, not a file"

blocks.text: The >&2 sends that message to the error stream rather than normal output, so a person piping the script's output into a file still sees the problem. Small habit, real difference when something fails at 3am.

rows: p exists and is a regular file
p exists and is a directory
you can read / write / execute it
the string is empty / is not empty
two numbers are equal (-lt -gt -le -ge for comparisons)
the command itself succeeded — exit code 0

blocks.title: = is for strings, -eq is for numbers
blocks.text: Using -eq on text produces an error, and using = on numbers compares them as text — so "10" = "9" is false but "10" -lt "9" is also false, for different reasons. Pick the operator that matches the kind of data, and quote both sides so an empty value does not break the test entirely.
Loops: the same work across a list

blocks.caption: for and while
lines: for host in web1 web2 db1; do

blocks.title: Loop over lines with while read, not for
blocks.text: for line in $(cat file) splits on every space, so a line containing spaces becomes several iterations. while read -r line; do ... done < file reads one whole line at a time. The -r stops backslashes being interpreted, which is what you want when reading data.
Functions: naming a piece of work

blocks.caption: Define once, call many times
lines: local name="$1"          # local keeps it out of the rest of the script

blocks.text: Functions take arguments the same way scripts do: $1, $2, $@. Use local for variables inside a function, otherwise they leak into the whole script and quietly overwrite something with the same name later.

blocks.title: Build a checker
steps: target="${1:-/etc}"                 # use $1, or /etc if none given
[ -e "$f" ] || continue          # skip when the pattern matched nothing
Run: echo $?                          (1, because you set it)
blocks.expected: A count for /etc, then a deliberate failure with a message on the error stream and exit code 1. That is a script that can be trusted inside a bigger pipeline, because it reports honestly when it cannot do its job.

cheatsheet: if [ condition ]; then ... elif ... else ... fi
-z empty string · -n non-empty · = string equality · -eq numeric equality
Quote both sides of a test so an empty value cannot break it
for x in a b c; do ... done — repeat over a list
while read -r line; do ... done < file — one whole line at a time
${1:-default} uses a default when the argument is missing
func() { ...; } defines a function; use local for its variables
>&2 sends a message to the error stream where it belongs

checkpoint.prompt: Which test is true only when the path exists and is a directory?
checkpoint.explanation: -d tests for a directory, -f for a regular file, -n only checks that the string is not empty, and -x checks the execute permission.

checkpoint.prompt: Why read lines with while read -r line rather than for line in $(cat file) ?

choices.A: for cannot read files at all
choices.C: while is faster on very large files
choices.D: The for version splits on spaces

checkpoint.explanation: A line containing spaces becomes several iterations. Word splitting again. while read takes one whole line per iteration, which is what 'for each line' actually means.

choices.A: Use the first argument, defaulting to /etc
choices.B: Require the first argument to be /etc
choices.C: Set the first argument permanently to /etc always

checkpoint.explanation: It is a default value. The script stays usable with no arguments while still accepting one.

choices.A: Writes them to the error stream
choices.C: It makes them appear in red text

checkpoint.explanation: They are still visible when normal output is redirected into a file or another command. Output and errors are separate streams. Keeping them separate means a failure is still noticed when someone captures the normal output somewhere else.
